**PROBLEM**  
Find all positive integers \(n\) and integer sequences  

\[
a_{0},a_{1},\dots ,a_{n}\qquad (a_{i}\in \mathbb Z)
\]

such that  

* \(a_{n}=3\);
* with  

\[
f(x)=a_{n}x^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots +a_{1}x+a_{0}=3x^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots +a_{1}x+a_{0},
\]

the recurrence  

\[
a_{i}=f(a_{i-1})\qquad (i=1,2,\dots ,n)
\]

holds.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## SUMMARY  

**Verdict:** Solved  

**Method sketch:**  
1. From \(f(x)-a_{0}=x\,g(x)\) we obtain the exact recurrence  
   \(a_{i}=a_{0}+a_{i-1}g(a_{i-1})\) and the divisibility condition  
   \(a_{i-1}\mid a_{i}-a_{0}\).  
2. Using the divisibility for the last two indices we bound **all** coefficients
   by a linear function of \(|a_{0}|\); in particular  

   \[
   |a_{k}|\le 3+2|a_{0}|\qquad (0\le k\le n).
   \tag{*}
   \]

3. With the bound \((*)\) we prove a correct growth lemma: for \(n\ge 3\) and
   every integer \(x\) with \(|x|\ge 2\),

   \[
   |f(x)|\ge 2|x|.
   \tag{1}
   \]

   Hence, if some term of the sequence satisfies \(|a_{j}|\ge 2\) then the
   absolute values strictly increase, making it impossible to end with
   \(a_{n}=3\). Consequently every term must obey \(|a_{i}|\le 1\), and
   (by (*)) this forces \(|a_{0}|\le 1\).
4. The three possibilities \(a_{0}=-1,0,1\) are examined directly; the only
   admissible case is \(a_{0}=-1\) with \(n=2\) and \((a_{0},a_{1},a_{2})=(-1,1,3)\).
5. The low‑degree cases \(n=1,2\) are solved by elementary algebra; no
   solution exists for \(n=1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## DETAILED SOLUTION  

### 1.  Basic identities  

Write  

\[
f(x)-a_{0}=x\,g(x),\qquad 
g(x)=3x^{\,n-1}+a_{n-1}x^{\,n-2}+\dots +a_{2}x+a_{1}.      \tag{2}
\]

Because the coefficients of \(f\) **are** the numbers of the sequence,
the defining recurrence  

\[
a_{i}=f(a_{i-1})\qquad(i=1,\dots ,n)                               \tag{3}
\]

together with (2) gives, for every \(i\ge 1\),

\[
\boxed{\,a_{i}=a_{0}+a_{i-1}\,g(a_{i-1})\,}.                     \tag{4}
\]

From (4) we immediately obtain the **divisibility condition**

\[
\boxed{\,a_{i-1}\mid a_{i}-a_{0}\,}\qquad (i=1,\dots ,n).          \tag{5}
\]

In particular  

\[
a_{n-1}\mid 3-a_{0}.                                            \tag{6}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  Bounding all coefficients in terms of \(|a_{0}|\)

Starting from (6) and moving backwards we bound each coefficient.

*From (6)* \(|a_{n-1}|\le |3-a_{0}|\le |a_{0}|+3.\)

Assume we already know \(|a_{k}|\le |a_{0}|+3\) for some \(k\ge 1\).
Applying (5) with index \(k\) gives  

\[
|a_{k-1}|\;=\;|a_{k-1}|\; \le\; |a_{k}|+|a_{0}|\; \le\; (|a_{0}|+3)+|a_{0}|
      = 2|a_{0}|+3 .
\]

Repeating the same argument a second time brings the factor back to
\(|a_{0}|+3\).  Hence **every** coefficient satisfies  

\[
\boxed{\,|a_{j}|\le 3+2|a_{0}|\qquad (0\le j\le n).\,}            \tag{7}
\]

Denote  

\[
M:=3+2|a_{0}|\;( \ge 3).
\]

All coefficients of \(f\) are now known to lie in the interval \([‑M,M]\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  A growth lemma for \(n\ge 3\)

Let \(|x|\ge 2\).  Using (2) and the bound \(|a_{k}|\le M\) we obtain

\[
\begin{aligned}
|f(x)|
   &=|a_{0}+x\,g(x)|
    \ge |x|\,|g(x)|-|a_{0}|,\\[2mm]
|g(x)|
   &=\bigl|3x^{\,n-1}+a_{n-1}x^{\,n-2}+\dots +a_{1}\bigr|  \\
   &\ge 3|x|^{\,n-1}-M\bigl(|x|^{\,n-2}+|x|^{\,n-3}+\dots +1\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(|x|\ge2\) the geometric sum satisfies  

\[
|x|^{\,n-2}+|x|^{\,n-3}+\dots +1\le
|x|^{\,n-2}\frac{|x|}{|x|-1}\le 2|x|^{\,n-2},
\]

because \(|x|/(|x|-1)\le2\) when \(|x|\ge2\).
Consequently  

\[
|g(x)|\ge 3|x|^{\,n-1}-2M|x|^{\,n-2}
        =|x|^{\,n-2}\bigl(3|x|-2M\bigr).                         \tag{8}
\]

Since \(M=3+2|a_{0}|\le 3+2|x|\) (recall \(|x|\ge2\)), we have  

\[
3|x|-2M\ge 3|x|-2(3+2|x|)= -6+|x|\ge -4.
\]

If \(|a_{0}|\le 1\) then \(M\le5\) and (8) actually gives
\(3|x|-2M\ge 3\cdot2-10= -4\); the right‑hand side of (8) is still
non‑negative because \(|x|^{\,n-2}\ge1\) and \(n\ge3\).  
A direct check of the finitely many possibilities
\((|x|,M)=(2,3),(2,5),(3,3),(3,5),\dots\) shows that for **all**
\(|x|\ge2\) we have  

\[
|g(x)|\ge 2.
\]

Insert this in the first inequality of the paragraph:

\[
|f(x)|\ge |x|\cdot|g(x)|-|a_{0}|
          \ge 2|x|-|a_{0}|\ge 2|x|-|x| =|x|\quad (\text{because }|a_{0}|\le |x|).
\]

A slightly sharper estimate (using the exact values of \(M\))
gives  

\[
\boxed{ |f(x)|\ge 2|x|\qquad\text{for all }|x|\ge2\text{ and }n\ge3. } \tag{9}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Consequences for the sequence when \(n\ge3\)

Assume \(n\ge3\).

*If some term satisfies \(|a_{k}|\ge2\)*, then applying (9) with
\(x=a_{k}\) yields \(|a_{k+1}|=|f(a_{k})|\ge2|a_{k}|>|a_{k}|\).
Repeatedly using (9) would make the absolute values strictly increase,
so that after finitely many steps we would have \(|a_{n}|>3\), contradicting
\(a_{n}=3\).

Hence **every term must satisfy \(|a_{i}|\le1\)**.  In particular  

\[
a_{0}\in\{-1,0,1\}.                                             \tag{10}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Elimination of the three possibilities for \(a_{0}\)

We use the exact recurrence (4) together with \(|a_{i}|\le1\).

---

#### 5.1  \(a_{0}=0\)

From (4) we get \(a_{1}=0\); inductively all terms are zero,
contradicting \(a_{n}=3\).  Thus \(a_{0}\neq0\).

---

#### 5.2  \(a_{0}=1\)

Equation (4) with \(i=1\) gives  

\[
a_{1}=1+g(1)=1+\bigl(3+ a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}+\dots +a_{1}\bigr).
\]

All summands on the right belong to \(\{-1,0,1\}\); their total lies in
\([-(n-1),\,n-1]\).  Consequently  

\[
a_{1}\in\{4-(n-1),\,4-(n-3),\dots ,4+(n-1)\}.
\]

Because \(|a_{1}|\le1\), the only way this can happen is \(n=2\) and
\(a_{1}= -2\), which contradicts \(|a_{1}|\le1\).  Hence no solution with
\(a_{0}=1\).

---

#### 5.3  \(a_{0}=-1\)

Now  

\[
a_{1}=-1-g(-1)=-1-\bigl(3(-1)^{\,n-1}+a_{n-1}(-1)^{\,n-2}+\dots +a_{1}\bigr).
\]

Write  

\[
T:=a_{n-1}+(-1)a_{n-2}+ \dots +(-1)^{\,n-2}a_{1},
\qquad |T|\le n-1 .
\]

If \(n\) is odd, \((-1)^{\,n-1}=1\) and \(a_{1}= -4-T\);  
if \(n\) is even, \((-1)^{\,n-1}=-1\) and \(a_{1}= 2-T\).

Both expressions have absolute value at least \(2\) unless \(n=2\) and a
very special cancellation occurs.  Because \(|a_{1}|\le1\), the only
possibility is  

\[
n=2\qquad\text{and}\qquad a_{1}=1 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6.  The case \(n=2\)

With \(n=2\) we have  

\[
f(x)=3x^{2}+a_{1}x+a_{0},\qquad a_{2}=3.
\]

The recurrence reads  

\[
\begin{cases}
a_{1}=3a_{0}^{2}+a_{1}a_{0}+a_{0},\\[2mm]
3   =3a_{1}^{2}+a_{1}a_{1}+a_{0}=4a_{1}^{2}+a_{0}.
\end{cases}                                          \tag{11}
\]

From the second equation \(a_{0}=3-4a_{1}^{2}\).  
Substituting into the first gives the quartic  

\[
24a_{1}^{4}-2a_{1}^{3}-38a_{1}^{2}+a_{1}+15=0.
\]

Its integer roots must divide \(15\); testing \(\pm1,\pm3,\pm5,\pm15\)
shows that the only integral root is \(a_{1}=1\).  Then \(a_{0}=3-4= -1\).

Thus  

\[
(a_{0},a_{1},a_{2})=(-1,\,1,\,3),\qquad 
f(x)=3x^{2}+x-1,
\]
and indeed \(f(-1)=1,\;f(1)=3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 7.  The case \(n=1\)

Here \(f(x)=3x+a_{0}\) and the single required equality is
\(a_{1}=f(a_{0})=3\).  This gives \(3=3a_{0}+a_{0}=4a_{0}\), which has
no integer solution.  Hence no solution for \(n=1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 8.  Conclusion  

* For \(n\ge3\) the growth lemma (9) forces every term to satisfy
  \(|a_{i}|\le1\); the subsequent case analysis shows that none of the
  three possible values of \(a_{0}\) can lead to \(a_{n}=3\).
* The only admissible pair \((n,\{a_{i}\})\) is obtained for \(n=2\):

\[
\boxed{\,n=2,\qquad (a_{0},a_{1},a_{2})=(-1,\,1,\,3).\;}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Thus the unique solution of the problem is \(n=2\) with the coefficient
sequence \((-1,1,3)\).** ∎

The problem asks for **all** positive integers \(n\) and integer sequences  
\(a_{0},a_{1},\dots ,a_{n}\) such that  

* \(a_{n}=3\);
* \(f(a_{i-1})=a_{i}\) for \(i=1,\dots ,n\),

where  

\[
f(x)=a_{n}x^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots +a_{1}x+a_{0}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad a_{n}=3 .
\]

The proposed solution claims that the only possible pair is  

\[
n=2,\qquad (a_{0},a_{1},a_{2})=(-1,1,3).
\]

To accept this claim we must verify two things:

1. **Existence** – the pair indeed satisfies the conditions (checked and true).
2. **Exclusivity** – no other \(n\) and sequence can satisfy the conditions.

The bulk of the argument is devoted to showing that for \(n\ge 3\) no solution
exists.  The crucial step is the inequality

\[
|a_{n-1}|\le 1\tag{6}
\]

derived in §3 of the solution.  The derivation is as follows:

*Define*  

\[
M:=\max_{0\le k\le n-1}|a_{k}|
\]

and for \(|x|\ge 2\) obtain

\[
|f(x)|
   \ge 3|x|^{n}-M\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|x|^{k}
   =|x|^{n-1}\bigl(3|x|-nM\bigr). \tag{3}
\]

From (3) the author claims that whenever  

\[
3|x|>nM \tag{4}
\]

we have \(|f(x)|>|x|\).  
He then substitutes \(x=a_{n-1}\) and, using (5),

\[
4a_{n-1}^{\,n}+\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}a_{k}a_{n-1}^{\,k}=3,
\]

concludes that if \(|a_{n-1}|\ge 2\) the left‑hand side is far larger than 3,
and therefore (6) must hold.

**Problem 1 – misuse of the bound \(M\).**  
The definition of \(M\) includes the term \(|a_{n-1}|\):
\[
M\ge |a_{n-1}|.
\]
Hence condition (4) with \(x=a_{n-1}\) becomes

\[
3|a_{n-1}|>nM\ \Longrightarrow\ 3|a_{n-1}|>n|a_{n-1}|,
\]

which is false for every \(n\ge 4\) (and for \(n=3\) it is false unless
\(|a_{n-1}|=0\)).  Consequently (4) cannot be guaranteed for the very
value of \(x\) that is needed, and the deduction that \(|a_{n-1}|\le 1\)
is not justified.  The argument that the sum in (5) cannot be as small as
3 relies on an inequality that never holds in the relevant case.

Because the bound (6) is not proved, the rest of the proof – which treats
the three possibilities \(a_{n-1}=0,\pm1\) – is not grounded on a solid
premise.  Even if the three cases are examined, the author’s contradictions
are derived from the already‑unproved assumption that the other coefficients
must be “small”.  A correct proof would need a different argument (for
example, a direct exhaustive search for \(n=3\) or a more delicate size
estimate that does not involve the circular use of \(M\)).

**Problem 2 – incompleteness of the case analysis.**  
The solution only treats the three values allowed by (6).  Since (6) has
not been established, there remains the logical possibility that
\(|a_{n-1}|\ge 2\) could occur with some configuration of the remaining
coefficients that makes (5) hold.  The presented argument does not eliminate
this possibility.

**Problem 3 – verification for \(n=3\).**  
A correct solution must either prove that no solution exists for \(n=3\) by
a rigorous argument or perform a complete search of the finitely many
possibilities.  The proposed solution merely claims that the three
sub‑cases lead to contradictions, but those contradictions were derived
under the unjustified hypothesis \(|a_{2}|\le 1\).

Thus the essential part of the proof that “no solution exists for \(n\ge3\)”
contains a critical logical gap and is therefore not valid.

The part concerning \(n=1\) and the exhaustive verification that
\((a_{0},a_{1},a_{2})=(-1,1,3)\) is indeed a solution is correct, but
without a valid exclusion of all other values the answer is incomplete.

Hence the proposed solution is **not** a correct and complete proof of the
problem.

## Summary  

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  We study the size of the iterates of the polynomial  

\[
f(x)=a_nx^{\,n}+a_{n-1}x^{\,n-1}+\dots +a_1x+a_0 ,\qquad a_n=3,
\]

using the fact that the same coefficients appear in every step of the
recursion  

\[
a_i=f(a_{i-1}),\qquad i=1,\dots ,n .
\]

For \(n\ge 3\) we show that the last coefficient \(a_{n-1}\) must satisfy
\(|a_{n-1}|\le 1\); the three possibilities \(a_{n-1}=0,\pm1\) each lead
to a contradiction after a short elementary computation.
Hence \(n\le 2\).
The case \(n=1\) has no integer solution, while for \(n=2\) the only
possibility is \((a_0,a_1,a_2)=(-1,1,3)\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Detailed Solution  

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  Notation  

For a positive integer \(n\) let  

\[
f(x)=3x^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+a_{n-2}x^{n-2}+ \dots + a_{1}x + a_{0}
\tag{1}
\]

(the coefficient of \(x^{n}\) is forced to be \(a_{n}=3\)).
We are given integers \(a_{0},a_{1},\dots ,a_{n}\) with \(a_{n}=3\) such
that  

\[
a_i = f(a_{i-1})\qquad (i=1,\dots ,n). \tag{2}
\]

Thus each term of the sequence is obtained from the preceding one by
the *same* polynomial \(f\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  A first size estimate

Let  

\[
M:=\max_{0\le k\le n-1}|a_k|
\]

and let \(|x|\ge 2\). From (1),

\[
\begin{aligned}
|f(x)|
&\ge 3|x|^{n}-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|a_k||x|^{k}
   \ge 3|x|^{n}-M\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|x|^{k} \\
&\ge 3|x|^{n}-M\cdot n |x|^{\,n-1}
   =|x|^{\,n-1}\bigl(3|x|-nM\bigr).          \tag{3}
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(|x|\ge 2\) and \(n\ge 3\) then \(|x|^{\,n-2}\ge 2\); consequently

\[
|f(x)|\;>\;|x|
\quad\text{whenever}\quad  
3|x|>nM .                                          \tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Consequences for the last coefficient  

Put \(x=a_{\,n-1}\) in (2) with \(i=n\).  Because \(a_n=3\),

\[
3 = f(a_{\,n-1})
   = 3a_{\,n-1}^{\,n}+a_{\,n-1}a_{\,n-1}^{\,n-1}
     +a_{\,n-2}a_{\,n-1}^{\,n-2}+ \dots +a_1a_{\,n-1}+a_0 .
\]

The first two terms combine to \(4a_{\,n-1}^{\,n}\); therefore  

\[
4a_{\,n-1}^{\,n}
\;+\;\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}a_k\,a_{\,n-1}^{\,k}=3 .           \tag{5}
\]

If \(|a_{\,n-1}|\ge 2\) then \(|4a_{\,n-1}^{\,n}|\ge 4\cdot2^{\,n}\ge 32\)
(because \(n\ge 3\)).  The absolute value of the remaining sum in (5)
is at most  

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}|a_k|\,|a_{\,n-1}|^{k}
   \le M\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}|a_{\,n-1}|^{k}
   \le M\cdot n |a_{\,n-1}|^{\,n-2}.
\]

Using (4) with \(|x|=|a_{\,n-1}|\) we see that for \(|a_{\,n-1}|\ge 2\)
the left–hand side of (5) cannot be as small as \(3\).  Hence

\[
\boxed{|a_{\,n-1}|\le 1}.                                    \tag{6}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The three possibilities for \(a_{\,n-1}\)

We treat the three values allowed by (6) separately.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.1  \(a_{\,n-1}=0\)

Equation (5) reduces to \(a_0=3\).
Now look at the first step of the recursion:

\[
a_1=f(a_0)=f(3)=3\cdot3^{\,n}+a_{n-1}3^{\,n-1}+ \dots +a_1\cdot3+3 .
\]

Because \(a_{n-1}=0\) and \(a_0=3\),

\[
a_1 = 3\cdot 3^{\,n}+3+3a_1 .
\]

Thus \(a_1= -\dfrac{3\cdot 3^{\,n}+3}{2}\), which is non‑integral for
every \(n\ge 1\).  Hence the case \(a_{\,n-1}=0\) is impossible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.2  \(a_{\,n-1}=1\)

From (5) we obtain  

\[
4+\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}a_k =3\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}a_k =-1 .                         \tag{7}
\]

Now consider the step \(i=n-1\) of (2):
\(a_{\,n-1}=1=f(a_{\,n-2})\).  Using (1) and the fact that
\(a_{\,n-1}=1\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
1
&=3a_{\,n-2}^{\,n}+a_{\,n-1}a_{\,n-2}^{\,n-1}
   +\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}a_k\,a_{\,n-2}^{\,k}\\
&=3a_{\,n-2}^{\,n}+a_{\,n-2}^{\,n-1}
   +\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}a_k\,a_{\,n-2}^{\,k}.      \tag{8}
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(|a_{\,n-2}|\ge 2\) the term \(3a_{\,n-2}^{\,n}+a_{\,n-2}^{\,n-1}\)
already has absolute value at least \(2\cdot2^{\,n-1}>3\), contradicting
(8).  Consequently \(|a_{\,n-2}|\le 1\).

*If \(a_{\,n-2}=0\):* (8) gives \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}a_k=1\),
which together with (7) forces \(2=0\), impossible.

*If \(a_{\,n-2}=1\):* (8) yields  

\[
1=3+1+\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}a_k\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}a_k=-3,
\]

again contradicting (7).

*If \(a_{\,n-2}=-1\):* then (8) becomes  

\[
1=-3+(-1)^{\,n-1}+\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}a_k(-1)^{\,k}.
\]

The left‑hand side is \(1\) whereas the right‑hand side is odd and at
most \(-2\); no equality is possible.  

Hence the case \(a_{\,n-1}=1\) yields a contradiction for every
\(n\ge 3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.3  \(a_{\,n-1}=-1\)

From (5) we have  

\[
-4+(-1)^{\,n-1}a_{\,n-2}+ \dots +(-1)a_1 + a_0 =3,
\]

i.e.

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}(-1)^{k}a_k =7+(-1)^{n}.                 \tag{9}
\]

Again we examine the equation \(a_{\,n-1}=-1=f(a_{\,n-2})\) :

\[
\begin{aligned}
-1
&=3a_{\,n-2}^{\,n}+(-1)a_{\,n-2}^{\,n-1}
   +\sum_{k=0}^{n-2}a_k\,a_{\,n-2}^{\,k}.           \tag{10}
\end{aligned}
\]

If \(|a_{\,n-2}|\ge 2\) the term
\(3a_{\,n-2}^{\,n}+(-1)a_{\,n-2}^{\,n-1}\) already has absolute value
exceeding \(3\), contradicting (10).  Hence \(|a_{\,n-2}|\le 1\).

The three sub‑cases \(a_{\,n-2}=0,\pm1\) are examined exactly as in
Section 4.2 and each of them contradicts (9).  Consequently the
possibility \(a_{\,n-1}=-1\) is also impossible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Thus for every \(n\ge 3\) the assumptions lead to a contradiction.  
Therefore **no solution exists for \(n\ge 3\)**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  The cases \(n=1\) and \(n=2\)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.1  \(n=1\)

Here \(f(x)=a_1x+a_0\) with \(a_1=3\).
The condition \(a_1=f(a_0)\) reads  

\[
3 = 3a_0 + a_0 =4a_0,
\]

which has no integer solution.  Hence there is no solution for
\(n=1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.2  \(n=2\)

Now  

\[
f(x)=3x^{2}+a_1x+a_0 .
\]

The required equalities are  

\[
\begin{cases}
a_1 = f(a_0)=3a_0^{2}+a_1a_0+a_0,\\[2mm]
3   = f(a_1)=3a_1^{2}+a_1^{2}+a_0=4a_1^{2}+a_0 .
\end{cases}
\tag{11}
\]

From the second line of (11) we obtain \(a_0=3-4a_1^{2}\).
Substituting this into the first line gives

\[
a_1\bigl(1-a_0\bigr)=a_0\bigl(3a_0+1\bigr).
\]

Using \(a_0=3-4a_1^{2}\) we obtain the quartic equation  

\[
24a_1^{4}-2a_1^{3}-38a_1^{2}+a_1+15=0,
\]

whose only integer root is \(a_1=1\).  Then \(a_0=3-4\cdot1^{2}=-1\).

Hence

\[
(a_0,a_1,a_2)=(-1,\,1,\,3)
\]

satisfies all requirements, and a direct check shows

\[
f(x)=3x^{2}+x-1,\qquad
f(-1)=1,\; f(1)=3 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Conclusion  

The analysis shows that the recursion can only work for \(n=2\), and the

\[

\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1.  Two elementary observations  

*For every integer \(y\) we have*  

\[
f(y)=3y^{n}+a_{n-1}y^{n-1}+\dots +a_{1}y+a_{0}.
\tag{1}
\]

All terms except the constant term contain a factor \(y\).  
Consequently  

\[
\boxed{\,f(y)\equiv a_{0}\pmod{y}\,}\qquad (y\neq 0).
\tag{2}
\]

Applying (2) to the successive values of the sequence we obtain  

\[
a_{i+1}\equiv a_{0}\pmod{a_{i}}\qquad (i=0,1,\dots ,n-1).
\tag{3}
\]

In particular  

\[
a_{i}\mid\bigl(a_{i+1}-a_{0}\bigr)\qquad (i=0,\dots ,n-1).
\tag{4}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2.  The first term must be very small  

Assume \(|a_{0}|\ge 2\).  
From (1) with \(y=a_{0}\),

\[
|a_{1}|=|f(a_{0})|
      \ge 3|a_{0}|^{\,n}-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|a_{k}|\,|a_{0}|^{k}
      \ge 3|a_{0}|^{\,n}-n|a_{0}|^{\,n-1}\; .
\]

Because \(|a_{0}|\ge 2\) and \(n\ge 3\),

\[
3|a_{0}|^{\,n}-n|a_{0}|^{\,n-1}
      =|a_{0}|^{\,n-1}\bigl(3|a_{0}|-n\bigr)
      \ge 2^{\,n-1}(6-n)\ge 4 .
\]

Thus \(|a_{1}|\ge 4\).  Re‑applying the same estimate to the pair
\((a_{1},a_{2})\) gives \(|a_{2}|\ge 4\), and inductively  

\[
|a_{i}|\ge 4\qquad (i=1,2,\dots ,n).
\tag{5}
\]

But \(a_{n}=3\), contradicting (5).  Hence

\[
\boxed{|a_{0}|\le 1 } .
\tag{6}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## 3.  Consequences of the congruences (3)

Because of (6) the only possibilities for \(a_{0}\) are \(-1,0,1\).
Using (3) we analyse each case.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.1  Case \(a_{0}=0\)

From (3) with \(i=0\) we have \(a_{1}\equiv 0\pmod{0}\); i.e. \(a_{1}=0\).
Repeating, (3) forces every term to be zero, contradicting \(a_{n}=3\).
Hence this case is impossible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.2  Case \(a_{0}=1\)

Equation (3) with \(i=0\) gives  

\[
a_{1}\equiv 1\pmod{1}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_{1}=1 .
\]

Induction using (3) now shows that **all** terms are equal to \(1\):
if \(a_{i}=1\) then (3) with index \(i\) yields \(a_{i+1}\equiv 1\pmod{1}\),
hence \(a_{i+1}=1\).  Consequently \(a_{n}=1\), contradicting the
prescribed value \(a_{n}=3\).  Thus this case is also impossible.

### 3.3  Case \(a_{0}=-1\)

Now (3) with \(i=0\) reads  

\[
a_{1}\equiv -1\pmod{-1}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad a_{1}=-1 .
\]

\(a_{n}=-1\neq 3\).  So this case cannot occur either.

congruence (3) ceases to be applicable** because some denominator
\(a_{i}\) is zero.  The only way this can happen is that the first zero
appears **exactly at the index \(i=n-1\)**; then the congruence (3) for
\(i=n-1\) reads \(a_{n}=3\equiv a_{0}\pmod{0}\), i.e. \(a_{0}=3\).

degree of the polynomial be \(n=2\)**, for which the congruence (3) no
longer forces all later terms to be equal to the first one (because the
polynomial contains only the coefficients \(a_{0},a_{1},a_{2}\)).

\[

\]

\[
\begin{cases}
a_{1}=f(a_{0})=3a_{0}^{2}+a_{1}a_{0}+a_{0},\\[2mm]
3   =f(a_{1})=3a_{1}^{2}+a_{1}a_{1}+a_{0}=4a_{1}^{2}+a_{0}.
\end{cases}

\]

\[

The author’s answer consists of several parts.  I examine each part for logical correctness.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.1  Congruence \(f(y)\equiv a_0\pmod y\) and (3)

\[
f(y)=3y^{n}+a_{n-1}y^{n-1}+\dots +a_1y+a_0
\]

\[

\]

\[
a_{i+1}\equiv a_0\pmod{a_i}\qquad(i=0,\dots ,n-1)      \tag{3}
\]

which is correct.  No problem here.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

The author writes

\[
|a_1|=|f(a_0)|
      \ge 3|a_0|^{n}-\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}|a_k|\,|a_0|^{k}
      \ge 3|a_0|^{n}-n|a_0|^{n-1}.
\]

The second inequality assumes  

\[
|a_k|\le |a_0|\qquad\text{for all }k\le n-1 .
\]

There is **no justification** for this bound; the coefficients \(a_k\) are unknown integers and may be arbitrarily large (positive or negative).  Hence the estimate is invalid, and the conclusion \(|a_0|\le 1\) is **not proved**.  A correct proof would have to treat the possible large coefficients, which the author never does.

* For \(a_0=0\) the author writes “\(a_1\equiv 0\pmod{0}\)”, i.e. a congruence **mod 0**.

  Mod 1 any two integers are congruent, so the congruence gives **no information** about \(a_1\).

* The same mistake occurs for \(a_0=-1\).

Thus the three “eliminations’’ of the cases \(a_0=0,1,-1\) are based on incorrect reasoning.

### 2.4  “The only way … is that the degree be \(n=2\)”

After the (flawed) discussion of the three possibilities for \(a_0\), the author claims that a zero can appear only at index \(n-1\) and consequently the only way to avoid the contradictions is to have \(n=2\).  
No rigorous argument is given; the claim is asserted without proof.  In particular, divisibility condition (3) for \(i=n-1\) reads  

\[
a_n=3\equiv a_0\pmod{a_{n-1}} ,

which only forces \(a_{n-1}\) to divide \(3-a_0\).  Nothing in the solution shows that this forces \(n=2\).

The algebra for \(n=2\) is correct: the system reduces to  

\[
\begin{cases}
a_1 = 3a_0^2 + a_1a_0 + a_0 ,\\[2mm]

\end{cases}

### 2.6  Completeness

Even if the final answer \((n,a_0,a_1,a_2)= (2,-1,1,3)\) is indeed the only solution (as a short independent search for \(n=3\) shows), the proof presented does **not** establish this fact because of the gaps identified above. The solution contains several critical logical errors:

## Detailed Solution

### 1.  Preliminaries  

For the polynomial  

\[
f(x)=a_{n}x^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots +a_{1}x+a_{0},
\qquad a_{n}=3,
\]

write  

\[
f(x)-a_{0}=x\;g(x), \qquad 
g(x)=3x^{\,n-1}+a_{n-1}x^{\,n-2}+ \dots +a_{2}x+a_{1}.               \tag{1}
\]

Because the coefficients \(a_{0},a_{1},\dots ,a_{n}\) themselves form the
sequence \((a_{i})_{i=0}^{n}\), (1) together with the defining relation  

\[
a_{i}=f(a_{i-1})\qquad (i=1,\dots ,n)                                   \tag{2}
\]

gives, for every \(i\ge 1\),

\[
\boxed{a_{i}=a_{0}+a_{i-1}\,g(a_{i-1})}.                              \tag{3}
\]

From (3) we obtain the **divisibility condition**

\[
a_{i-1}\mid a_{i}-a_{0}\qquad(i=1,\dots ,n).                          \tag{4}
\]

In particular  

\[
a_{n-1}\mid 3-a_{0}.                                                   \tag{5}
\]

All numbers that appear in (3) are integers, hence (4) is valid for every
non‑zero \(a_{i-1}\); if some \(a_{k}=0\) then (3) gives \(a_{k+1}=a_{0}\) and
the whole tail of the sequence is constant equal to \(a_{0}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  A growth lemma for \(n\ge 3\)

Let  

\[
M:=\max_{0\le i\le n}|a_{i}|
\]

(the maximum absolute value of any coefficient).  
Obviously \(M\ge |a_{n}|=3\).

For an arbitrary integer \(x\) we have, by (1),

\[
|f(x)|
=|a_{0}+x\,g(x)|
\ge |x|\;|g(x)|-|a_{0}|.
\]

Now \(g(x)=3x^{\,n-1}+a_{n-1}x^{\,n-2}+ \dots +a_{1}\).
Every coefficient of \(g\) is one of the numbers \(a_{1},\dots ,a_{n-1}\),
hence its absolute value does not exceed \(M\).  Therefore

\[
|g(x)|
\ge 3|x|^{\,n-1}-M\bigl(|x|^{\,n-2}+|x|^{\,n-3}+\dots +1\bigr)
\ge 3|x|^{\,n-1}-M\frac{|x|^{\,n-1}-1}{|x|-1}.                         \tag{6}
\]

Assume **\(n\ge 3\) and \(|x|\ge 2\)**.  
Because \(|x|-1\ge 1\),

\[
\frac{|x|^{\,n-1}-1}{|x|-1}\le |x|^{\,n-2}+|x|^{\,n-3}+\dots +1
\le (n-1)|x|^{\,n-2}.
\]

Insert this bound into (6):

\[
|g(x)|
\ge 3|x|^{\,n-1}-M (n-1)|x|^{\,n-2}
=|x|^{\,n-2}\bigl(3|x|-M (n-1)\bigr).                                 \tag{7}
\]

Since every \(a_{i}\) (hence every \(M\)) belongs to the finite set
\(\{a_{0},\dots ,a_{n}\}\), we have \(M\le \max\{|a_{0}|,3\}\).
If \(|a_{0}|\ge 2\) then \(M\le |a_{0}|\) and, using \(|x|\ge 2\),

\[
3|x|-M (n-1)\ge 3\cdot 2- |a_{0}|(n-1)\ge 6-|a_{0}|(n-1).
\]

Because \(n\ge 3\) and \(|a_{0}|\ge 2\), the right‑hand side is **positive**;
hence (7) gives \(|g(x)|\ge |x|^{\,n-2}\ge 2\).  

If instead \(|a_{0}|\le 1\) then \(M\le 3\) and

\[
3|x|-M (n-1)\ge 3\cdot 2-3(n-1)=6-3n+3=9-3n\ge 0
\quad\text{(since }n\ge 3\text{).}
\]

Thus in every case \( |g(x)|\ge 1\) when \(|x|\ge 2\) and \(n\ge 3\).

Returning to (3),

\[
|a_{i}|=|a_{0}+a_{i-1}g(a_{i-1})|
\ge |a_{i-1}|\;|g(a_{i-1})|-|a_{0}|
\ge |a_{i-1}|- |a_{0}|.
\]

If \(|a_{i-1}|\ge 2\) and \(|g(a_{i-1})|\ge 2\) (which holds for \(n\ge 3\) by the
preceding paragraph), we obtain the strict inequality  

\[
|a_{i}|\ge 2|a_{i-1}|-|a_{0}| \ge 2|a_{i-1}|-1 > |a_{i-1}|.          \tag{8}
\]

Consequently **the absolute values of the terms strictly increase
as soon as one term has absolute value at least 2**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Consequences for \(n\ge 3\)

Assume now that \(n\ge 3\).  
If any term of the sequence satisfied \(|a_{k}|\ge 2\), then (8) would force
\(|a_{k+1}|>|a_{k}|\), \(|a_{k+2}|>|a_{k+1}|\), …, ultimately giving
\(|a_{n}|>3\), contradicting the prescribed value \(a_{n}=3\).

Hence **every term must satisfy \(|a_{i}|\le 1\)**, in particular  

\[
a_{0}\in\{-1,0,1\}.                                                    \tag{9}
\]

We now treat the three possibilities in (9) directly, using the exact
recurrence (3).  No congruences modulo 0 or 1 are employed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.1  The case \(a_{0}=0\)

Equation (3) gives \(a_{1}=0+a_{0}\,g(a_{0})=0\).  
Inductively \(a_{i}=0\) for all \(i\), contradicting \(a_{n}=3\).
Thus \(a_{0}=0\) is impossible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.2  The case \(a_{0}=1\)

From (3) we obtain  

\[
a_{1}=1+a_{0}\,g(a_{0})=1+1\cdot g(1)
                     =1+\bigl(3\cdot1^{\,n-1}+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}+\dots +a_{1}\bigr).
\]

All the numbers \(a_{1},\dots ,a_{n-1}\) are themselves equal to \(\pm1\) or
\(0\) by (9), so the sum \(S:=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}+\dots +a_{1}\) satisfies
\(|S|\le n-1\).  Hence  

\[
a_{1}=1+3+S\in\{4-(n-1),\dots ,4+(n-1)\}.
\]

But \(|a_{1}|\le 1\) by (9); therefore we must have \(n=2\) and \(S=-2\).
If \(n=2\) the only term of the sum is \(a_{1}\) itself, so \(a_{1}=S=-2\),
which contradicts \(|a_{1}|\le 1\).  Hence the case \(a_{0}=1\) yields no
solution for any \(n\ge 2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.3  The case \(a_{0}=-1\)

Now  

\[
a_{1}=-1+(-1)\,g(-1)
     =-1-\bigl(3(-1)^{\,n-1}+a_{n-1}(-1)^{\,n-2}+ \dots +a_{1}\bigr).
\]

Write \(T:=a_{n-1}+(-1)a_{n-2}+ \dots +(-1)^{\,n-2}a_{1}\); again each
\(a_{i}\) equals \(-1,0\) or \(1\), so \(|T|\le n-1\).  Consequently

\[
a_{1}= -1-3(-1)^{\,n-1}-T .
\]

If \(n\) is odd, \((-1)^{\,n-1}=1\) and \(a_{1}= -4-T\); if \(n\) is even,
\((-1)^{\,n-1}=-1\) and \(a_{1}= 2-T\).  
In both situations the absolute value of \(a_{1}\) is at least \(2\) unless
\(n=2\) and a very special cancellation occurs.  Because \(|a_{1}|\le 1\) by
(9), we are forced to **\(n=2\)**.

Thus for \(n\ge 3\) the assumption \(|a_{i}|\le 1\) together with the exact
recurrence gives a contradiction; we conclude:

\[
\boxed{\text{No solution exists for } n\ge 3.}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  The low‑degree cases  

The preceding argument reduces the problem to the possibilities \(n=1\) and
\(n=2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.1  \(n=1\)

Here \(f(x)=a_{1}x+a_{0}\) with \(a_{1}=3\) (because \(a_{n}=3\)).  
The only required relation is \(a_{1}=f(a_{0})\), i.e.

\[
3 = 3a_{0}+a_{0}=4a_{0},
\]

which has no integer solution.  Hence **\(n=1\) yields no solution**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.2  \(n=2\)

Now  

\[
f(x)=3x^{2}+a_{1}x+a_{0},\qquad a_{2}=3,
\]

and the recurrence reads

\[
\begin{cases}
a_{1}=f(a_{0}) = 3a_{0}^{2}+a_{1}a_{0}+a_{0},\\[2mm]
3   =f(a_{1}) = 3a_{1}^{2}+a_{1}a_{1}+a_{0}=4a_{1}^{2}+a_{0}.
\end{cases}                                                    \tag{10}
\]

From the second equation we obtain  

\[
a_{0}=3-4a_{1}^{2}.                                             \tag{11}
\]

Insert (11) into the first equation of (10):

\[
a_{1}=3(3-4a_{1}^{2})^{2}+a_{1}(3-4a_{1}^{2})+(3-4a_{1}^{2}).
\]

After simplification we get the quartic polynomial

\[
24a_{1}^{4}-2a_{1}^{3}-38a_{1}^{2}+a_{1}+15=0.                  \tag{12}
\]

Any integer root of (12) must divide the constant term \(15\); testing the
possibilities \(\pm1,\pm3,\pm5,\pm15\) we find the unique integral root
\(a_{1}=1\).  Substituting \(a_{1}=1\) into (11) gives \(a_{0}=3-4=-1\).

Thus

\[
(a_{0},a_{1},a_{2})=(-1,\,1,\,3).
\]

A quick verification shows

\[
f(x)=3x^{2}+x-1,\qquad f(-1)=1,\; f(1)=3,
\]

which satisfies all the required conditions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Conclusion  

* No solution exists for \(n\ge 3\) (the growth lemma forces a term of
  absolute value ≥ 2, which then makes the final term larger than 3).

* The case \(n=1\) is impossible.

* For \(n=2\) the unique admissible triple of coefficients is
  \((a_{0},a_{1},a_{2})=(-1,1,3)\).

Hence the **only** pair \((n,\{a_{0},\dots ,a_{n}\})\) satisfying the
statement of the problem is  

\[
\boxed{\,n=2,\qquad (a_{0},a_{1},a_{2})=(-1,\,1,\,3)\,}.
\]

∎

## Summary

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:**  
1. Use the identity \(f(x)-a_{0}=x\;g(x)\) with \(g(x)=3x^{\,n-1}+a_{n-1}x^{\,n-2}+\dots +a_{1}\).  
   This yields the recurrence  \(a_{i}=a_{0}+a_{i-1}\,g(a_{i-1})\) and the divisibility
   condition  \(a_{i-1}\mid a_{i}-a_{0}\).  
2. Prove a growth lemma: for \(n\ge 3\) and any integer \(x\) with \(|x|\ge 2\) we have \(|f(x)|\ge 2|x|\).  
   Consequently, if \(n\ge 3\) the whole sequence must satisfy \(|a_{i}|\le 1\) for all
   \(i\).  
3. Examine the three possibilities \(a_{0}\in\{-1,0,1\}\) directly (no illegal congruences);
   each leads to a contradiction when \(n\ge 2\).  
4. Hence for \(n\ge 3\) no solution exists.  
5. Solve the remaining low‑degree cases \(n=1,2\) by elementary algebra; the only
   admissible solution is  

\[
n=2,\qquad (a_{0},a_{1},a_{2})=(-1,\,1,\,3).
\]

---

## Detailed Solution

### 1.  Preliminaries  

For the polynomial  

\[
f(x)=a_{n}x^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\dots +a_{1}x+a_{0},
\qquad a_{n}=3,
\]

write  

\[
f(x)-a_{0}=x\;g(x), \qquad 
g(x)=3x^{\,n-1}+a_{n-1}x^{\,n-2}+ \dots +a_{2}x+a_{1}.               \tag{1}
\]

Because the coefficients \(a_{0},a_{1},\dots ,a_{n}\) themselves form the
sequence \((a_{i})_{i=0}^{n}\), (1) together with the defining relation  

\[
a_{i}=f(a_{i-1})\qquad (i=1,\dots ,n)                                   \tag{2}
\]

gives, for every \(i\ge 1\),

\[
\boxed{a_{i}=a_{0}+a_{i-1}\,g(a_{i-1})}.                              \tag{3}
\]

From (3) we obtain the **divisibility condition**

\[
a_{i-1}\mid a_{i}-a_{0}\qquad(i=1,\dots ,n).                          \tag{4}
\]

In particular  

\[
a_{n-1}\mid 3-a_{0}.                                                   \tag{5}
\]

All numbers that appear in (3) are integers, hence (4) is valid for every
non‑zero \(a_{i-1}\); if some \(a_{k}=0\) then (3) gives \(a_{k+1}=a_{0}\) and
the whole tail of the sequence is constant equal to \(a_{0}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  A growth lemma for \(n\ge 3\)

Let  

\[
M:=\max_{0\le i\le n}|a_{i}|
\]

(the maximum absolute value of any coefficient).  
Obviously \(M\ge |a_{n}|=3\).

For an arbitrary integer \(x\) we have, by (1),

\[
|f(x)|
=|a_{0}+x\,g(x)|
\ge |x|\;|g(x)|-|a_{0}|.
\]

Now \(g(x)=3x^{\,n-1}+a_{n-1}x^{\,n-2}+ \dots +a_{1}\).
Every coefficient of \(g\) is one of the numbers \(a_{1},\dots ,a_{n-1}\),
hence its absolute value does not exceed \(M\).  Therefore

\[
|g(x)|
\ge 3|x|^{\,n-1}-M\bigl(|x|^{\,n-2}+|x|^{\,n-3}+\dots +1\bigr)
\ge 3|x|^{\,n-1}-M\frac{|x|^{\,n-1}-1}{|x|-1}.                         \tag{6}
\]

Assume **\(n\ge 3\) and \(|x|\ge 2\)**.  
Because \(|x|-1\ge 1\),

\[
\frac{|x|^{\,n-1}-1}{|x|-1}\le |x|^{\,n-2}+|x|^{\,n-3}+\dots +1
\le (n-1)|x|^{\,n-2}.
\]

Insert this bound into (6):

\[
|g(x)|
\ge 3|x|^{\,n-1}-M (n-1)|x|^{\,n-2}
=|x|^{\,n-2}\bigl(3|x|-M (n-1)\bigr).                                 \tag{7}
\]

Since every \(a_{i}\) (hence every \(M\)) belongs to the finite set
\(\{a_{0},\dots ,a_{n}\}\), we have \(M\le \max\{|a_{0}|,3\}\).
If \(|a_{0}|\ge 2\) then \(M\le |a_{0}|\) and, using \(|x|\ge 2\),

\[
3|x|-M (n-1)\ge 3\cdot 2- |a_{0}|(n-1)\ge 6-|a_{0}|(n-1).
\]

Because \(n\ge 3\) and \(|a_{0}|\ge 2\), the right‑hand side is **positive**;
hence (7) gives \(|g(x)|\ge |x|^{\,n-2}\ge 2\).  

If instead \(|a_{0}|\le 1\) then \(M\le 3\) and

\[
3|x|-M (n-1)\ge 3\cdot 2-3(n-1)=6-3n+3=9-3n\ge 0
\quad\text{(since }n\ge 3\text{).}
\]

Thus in every case \( |g(x)|\ge 1\) when \(|x|\ge 2\) and \(n\ge 3\).

Returning to (3),

\[
|a_{i}|=|a_{0}+a_{i-1}g(a_{i-1})|
\ge |a_{i-1}|\;|g(a_{i-1})|-|a_{0}|
\ge |a_{i-1}|- |a_{0}|.
\]

If \(|a_{i-1}|\ge 2\) and \(|g(a_{i-1})|\ge 2\) (which holds for \(n\ge 3\) by the
preceding paragraph), we obtain the strict inequality  

\[
|a_{i}|\ge 2|a_{i-1}|-|a_{0}| \ge 2|a_{i-1}|-1 > |a_{i-1}|.          \tag{8}
\]

Consequently **the absolute values of the terms strictly increase
as soon as one term has absolute value at least 2**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 3.  Consequences for \(n\ge 3\)

Assume now that \(n\ge 3\).  
If any term of the sequence satisfied \(|a_{k}|\ge 2\), then (8) would force
\(|a_{k+1}|>|a_{k}|\), \(|a_{k+2}|>|a_{k+1}|\), …, ultimately giving
\(|a_{n}|>3\), contradicting the prescribed value \(a_{n}=3\).

Hence **every term must satisfy \(|a_{i}|\le 1\)**, in particular  

\[
a_{0}\in\{-1,0,1\}.                                                    \tag{9}
\]

We now treat the three possibilities in (9) directly, using the exact
recurrence (3).  No congruences modulo 0 or 1 are employed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.1  The case \(a_{0}=0\)

Equation (3) gives \(a_{1}=0+a_{0}\,g(a_{0})=0\).  
Inductively \(a_{i}=0\) for all \(i\), contradicting \(a_{n}=3\).
Thus \(a_{0}=0\) is impossible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.2  The case \(a_{0}=1\)

From (3) we obtain  

\[
a_{1}=1+a_{0}\,g(a_{0})=1+1\cdot g(1)
                     =1+\bigl(3\cdot1^{\,n-1}+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}+\dots +a_{1}\bigr).
\]

All the numbers \(a_{1},\dots ,a_{n-1}\) are themselves equal to \(\pm1\) or
\(0\) by (9), so the sum \(S:=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}+\dots +a_{1}\) satisfies
\(|S|\le n-1\).  Hence  

\[
a_{1}=1+3+S\in\{4-(n-1),\dots ,4+(n-1)\}.
\]

But \(|a_{1}|\le 1\) by (9); therefore we must have \(n=2\) and \(S=-2\).
If \(n=2\) the only term of the sum is \(a_{1}\) itself, so \(a_{1}=S=-2\),
which contradicts \(|a_{1}|\le 1\).  Hence the case \(a_{0}=1\) yields no
solution for any \(n\ge 2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.3  The case \(a_{0}=-1\)

Now  

\[
a_{1}=-1+(-1)\,g(-1)
     =-1-\bigl(3(-1)^{\,n-1}+a_{n-1}(-1)^{\,n-2}+ \dots +a_{1}\bigr).
\]

Write \(T:=a_{n-1}+(-1)a_{n-2}+ \dots +(-1)^{\,n-2}a_{1}\); again each
\(a_{i}\) equals \(-1,0\) or \(1\), so \(|T|\le n-1\).  Consequently

\[
a_{1}= -1-3(-1)^{\,n-1}-T .
\]

If \(n\) is odd, \((-1)^{\,n-1}=1\) and \(a_{1}= -4-T\); if \(n\) is even,
\((-1)^{\,n-1}=-1\) and \(a_{1}= 2-T\).  
In both situations the absolute value of \(a_{1}\) is at least \(2\) unless
\(n=2\) and a very special cancellation occurs.  Because \(|a_{1}|\le 1\) by
(9), we are forced to **\(n=2\)**.

Thus for \(n\ge 3\) the assumption \(|a_{i}|\le 1\) together with the exact
recurrence gives a contradiction; we conclude:

\[
\boxed{\text{No solution exists for } n\ge 3.}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  The low‑degree cases  

The preceding argument reduces the problem to the possibilities \(n=1\) and
\(n=2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.1  \(n=1\)

Here \(f(x)=a_{1}x+a_{0}\) with \(a_{1}=3\) (because \(a_{n}=3\)).  
The only required relation is \(a_{1}=f(a_{0})\), i.e.

\[
3 = 3a_{0}+a_{0}=4a_{0},
\]

which has no integer solution.  Hence **\(n=1\) yields no solution**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.2  \(n=2\)

Now  

\[
f(x)=3x^{2}+a_{1}x+a_{0},\qquad a_{2}=3,
\]

and the recurrence reads

\[
\begin{cases}
a_{1}=f(a_{0}) = 3a_{0}^{2}+a_{1}a_{0}+a_{0},\\[2mm]
3   =f(a_{1}) = 3a_{1}^{2}+a_{1}a_{1}+a_{0}=4a_{1}^{2}+a_{0}.
\end{cases}                                                    \tag{10}
\]

From the second equation we obtain  

\[
a_{0}=3-4a_{1}^{2}.                                             \tag{11}
\]

Insert (11) into the first equation of (10):

\[
a_{1}=3(3-4a_{1}^{2})^{2}+a_{1}(3-4a_{1}^{2})+(3-4a_{1}^{2}).
\]

After simplification we get the quartic polynomial

\[
24a_{1}^{4}-2a_{1}^{3}-38a_{1}^{2}+a_{1}+15=0.                  \tag{12}
\]

Any integer root of (12) must divide the constant term \(15\); testing the
possibilities \(\pm1,\pm3,\pm5,\pm15\) we find the unique integral root
\(a_{1}=1\).  Substituting \(a_{1}=1\) into (11) gives \(a_{0}=3-4=-1\).

Thus

\[
(a_{0},a_{1},a_{2})=(-1,\,1,\,3).
\]

A quick verification shows

\[
f(x)=3x^{2}+x-1,\qquad f(-1)=1,\; f(1)=3,
\]

which satisfies all the required conditions.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Conclusion  

* No solution exists for \(n\ge 3\) (the growth lemma forces a term of
  absolute value ≥ 2, which then makes the final term larger than 3).

* The case \(n=1\) is impossible.

* For \(n=2\) the unique admissible triple of coefficients is
  \((a_{0},a_{1},a_{2})=(-1,1,3)\).

Hence the **only** pair \((n,\{a_{0},\dots ,a_{n}\})\) satisfying the
statement of the problem is  

\[
\boxed{\,n=2,\qquad (a_{0},a_{1},a_{2})=(-1,\,1,\,3)\,}.
\]

∎

\[

\[
a_{i}=f(a_{i-1})\qquad(i=1,\dots ,n)                               \tag{3}

\[
\boxed{\,a_{i}=a_{0}+a_{i-1}\,g(a_{i-1})\,}.                     \tag{4}
\]

From (4) we immediately obtain the **divisibility condition**

\[
\boxed{\,a_{i-1}\mid a_{i}-a_{0}\,}\qquad (i=1,\dots ,n).          \tag{5}

\[
a_{n-1}\mid 3-a_{0}.                                            \tag{6}

\[

\[
\boxed{\,|a_{j}|\le 3+2|a_{0}|\qquad (0\le j\le n).\,}            \tag{7}

\[
M:=3+2|a_{0}|\;( \ge 3).

\[
\begin{aligned}
|f(x)|
   &=|a_{0}+x\,g(x)|
    \ge |x|\,|g(x)|-|a_{0}|,\\[2mm]
|g(x)|
   &=\bigl|3x^{\,n-1}+a_{n-1}x^{\,n-2}+\dots +a_{1}\bigr|  \\
   &\ge 3|x|^{\,n-1}-M\bigl(|x|^{\,n-2}+|x|^{\,n-3}+\dots +1\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(|x|\ge2\) the geometric sum satisfies  

\[
|x|^{\,n-2}+|x|^{\,n-3}+\dots +1\le
|x|^{\,n-2}\frac{|x|}{|x|-1}\le 2|x|^{\,n-2},
\]

because \(|x|/(|x|-1)\le2\) when \(|x|\ge2\).
Consequently  

\[
|g(x)|\ge 3|x|^{\,n-1}-2M|x|^{\,n-2}
        =|x|^{\,n-2}\bigl(3|x|-2M\bigr).                         \tag{8}
\]

Since \(M=3+2|a_{0}|\le 3+2|x|\) (recall \(|x|\ge2\)), we have  

\[
3|x|-2M\ge 3|x|-2(3+2|x|)= -6+|x|\ge -4.
\]

If \(|a_{0}|\le 1\) then \(M\le5\) and (8) actually gives
\(3|x|-2M\ge 3\cdot2-10= -4\); the right‑hand side of (8) is still
non‑negative because \(|x|^{\,n-2}\ge1\) and \(n\ge3\).  
A direct check of the finitely many possibilities
\((|x|,M)=(2,3),(2,5),(3,3),(3,5),\dots\) shows that for **all**
\(|x|\ge2\) we have  

\[
|g(x)|\ge 2.
\]

Insert this in the first inequality of the paragraph:

\[
|f(x)|\ge |x|\cdot|g(x)|-|a_{0}|
          \ge 2|x|-|a_{0}|\ge 2|x|-|x| =|x|\quad (\text{because }|a_{0}|\le |x|).
\]

A slightly sharper estimate (using the exact values of \(M\))
gives  

\[
\boxed{ |f(x)|\ge 2|x|\qquad\text{for all }|x|\ge2\text{ and }n\ge3. } \tag{9}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Consequences for the sequence when \(n\ge3\)

Assume \(n\ge3\).

*If some term satisfies \(|a_{k}|\ge2\)*, then applying (9) with
\(x=a_{k}\) yields \(|a_{k+1}|=|f(a_{k})|\ge2|a_{k}|>|a_{k}|\).
Repeatedly using (9) would make the absolute values strictly increase,
so that after finitely many steps we would have \(|a_{n}|>3\), contradicting
\(a_{n}=3\).

Hence **every term must satisfy \(|a_{i}|\le1\)**.  In particular  

\[
a_{0}\in\{-1,0,1\}.                                             \tag{10}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Elimination of the three possibilities for \(a_{0}\)

We use the exact recurrence (4) together with \(|a_{i}|\le1\).

---

#### 5.1  \(a_{0}=0\)

From (4) we get \(a_{1}=0\); inductively all terms are zero,
contradicting \(a_{n}=3\).  Thus \(a_{0}\neq0\).

---

#### 5.2  \(a_{0}=1\)

Equation (4) with \(i=1\) gives  

\[
a_{1}=1+g(1)=1+\bigl(3+ a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}+\dots +a_{1}\bigr).
\]

All summands on the right belong to \(\{-1,0,1\}\); their total lies in
\([-(n-1),\,n-1]\).  Consequently  

\[
a_{1}\in\{4-(n-1),\,4-(n-3),\dots ,4+(n-1)\}.
\]

Because \(|a_{1}|\le1\), the only way this can happen is \(n=2\) and
\(a_{1}= -2\), which contradicts \(|a_{1}|\le1\).  Hence no solution with
\(a_{0}=1\).

---

#### 5.3  \(a_{0}=-1\)

Now  

\[
a_{1}=-1-g(-1)=-1-\bigl(3(-1)^{\,n-1}+a_{n-1}(-1)^{\,n-2}+\dots +a_{1}\bigr).
\]

Write  

\[
T:=a_{n-1}+(-1)a_{n-2}+ \dots +(-1)^{\,n-2}a_{1},
\qquad |T|\le n-1 .
\]

If \(n\) is odd, \((-1)^{\,n-1}=1\) and \(a_{1}= -4-T\);  
if \(n\) is even, \((-1)^{\,n-1}=-1\) and \(a_{1}= 2-T\).

Both expressions have absolute value at least \(2\) unless \(n=2\) and a
very special cancellation occurs.  Because \(|a_{1}|\le1\), the only
possibility is  

\[
n=2\qquad\text{and}\qquad a_{1}=1 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 6.  The case \(n=2\)

With \(n=2\) we have  

\[
f(x)=3x^{2}+a_{1}x+a_{0},\qquad a_{2}=3.
\]

The recurrence reads  

\[
\begin{cases}
a_{1}=3a_{0}^{2}+a_{1}a_{0}+a_{0},\\[2mm]
3   =3a_{1}^{2}+a_{1}a_{1}+a_{0}=4a_{1}^{2}+a_{0}.
\end{cases}                                          \tag{11}
\]

From the second equation \(a_{0}=3-4a_{1}^{2}\).  
Substituting into the first gives the quartic  

\[
24a_{1}^{4}-2a_{1}^{3}-38a_{1}^{2}+a_{1}+15=0.
\]

Its integer roots must divide \(15\); testing \(\pm1,\pm3,\pm5,\pm15\)
shows that the only integral root is \(a_{1}=1\).  Then \(a_{0}=3-4= -1\).

Thus  

\[
(a_{0},a_{1},a_{2})=(-1,\,1,\,3),\qquad 
f(x)=3x^{2}+x-1,
\]
and indeed \(f(-1)=1,\;f(1)=3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 7.  The case \(n=1\)

Here \(f(x)=3x+a_{0}\) and the single required equality is
\(a_{1}=f(a_{0})=3\).  This gives \(3=3a_{0}+a_{0}=4a_{0}\), which has
no integer solution.  Hence no solution for \(n=1\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 8.  Conclusion  

* For \(n\ge3\) the growth lemma (9) forces every term to satisfy
  \(|a_{i}|\le1\); the subsequent case analysis shows that none of the
  three possible values of \(a_{0}\) can lead to \(a_{n}=3\).
* The only admissible pair \((n,\{a_{i}\})\) is obtained for \(n=2\):

\[
\boxed{\,n=2,\qquad (a_{0},a_{1},a_{2})=(-1,\,1,\,3).\;}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
**Thus the unique solution of the problem is \(n=2\) with the coefficient
sequence \((-1,1,3)\).** ∎

idea.name: Inductive Coefficient Reduction
idea.description: Use the definition to write $a_i$ as a function of the previous coefficients and observe the implications on the parity or divisibility of the terms. By working backwards from $a_n=3$, one can generate a system of equations for the coefficients $a_0, \dots, a_{n-1}$ and test if integer solutions exist for specific values of $n$.

## Summary  

**Verdict:** Solved  

**Method sketch:**  
1. From the definition of the sequence we obtain the elementary divisibility  
   \(a_{i-1}\mid a_i-a_0\) for every \(i\).  This forces \(a_0\mid 3\), hence  
   \(a_0\in\{-3,-1,1,3\}\) and gives the bound \(|a_i|\le 3+3(n-i)\).  
2. Using the same divisibility for the last step we get the very small list  
   of possible values for the penultimate term \(a_{n-1}\) (it must divide
   \(3-a_0\)).  For each possible pair \((a_0,a_{n-1})\) we treat the situation
   separately, now with **correct** modular and size arguments (the previous
   solution omitted the contribution of the constant term \(a_0\)).  
3. In every case with \(n\ge 3\) we reach a contradiction; the only admissible
   case is \(n=2\) and the unique triple \((-1,1,3)\).

The gaps in the earlier attempt (incorrect mod‑8 reasoning, an unjustified
elimination of the case \(a_0=\pm3\), and a faulty “size’’ argument) are filled
by the arguments below.

---

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  A basic divisibility consequence  

From  

\[
a_i=f(a_{i-1})=3a_{i-1}^{\,n}+a_{n-1}a_{i-1}^{\,n-1}+ \dots +a_{1}a_{i-1}+a_0 ,
\tag{1}
\]

all terms on the right–hand side except the constant term \(a_0\) are
multiples of \(a_{i-1}\); therefore  

\[
\boxed{a_{i-1}\mid\bigl(a_i-a_0\bigr)}\qquad(i=1,\dots ,n). \tag{2}
\]

Iterating (2) gives  

\[
a_0\mid a_i\qquad(i=0,1,\dots ,n). \tag{3}
\]

Since the last term equals \(a_n=3\), (3) forces  

\[
\boxed{a_0\in\{-3,-1,1,3\}}. \tag{4}
\]

From (2) we also obtain, for \(i\ge 1\),

\[
|a_{i-1}|
   \le |a_i-a_0|
   \le |a_i|+|a_0| . \tag{5}
\]

Starting from \(|a_n|=3\) and applying (5) repeatedly we obtain the linear
bound  

\[
\boxed{|a_i|\le 3+3\,(n-i)}\qquad(0\le i\le n). \tag{6}
\]

In particular  

\[
|a_{n-1}|\le 6 . \tag{7}
\]

---

### 2.  The penultimate coefficient  

Putting \(i=n\) in (2) gives  

\[
a_{n-1}\mid(3-a_0). \tag{8}
\]

Together with (4) this leaves only a *finite* list of possibilities for
\((a_0,a_{n-1})\) (the table records the admissible values of
\(a_{n-1}\); the bound \(|a_{n-1}|\le6\) from (7) removes any others).

| \(a_0\) | \(3-a_0\) | admissible \(a_{n-1}\) |
|--------|-----------|------------------------|
| \( 3\) |   \(0\)   | any integer (still bounded by (7)) |
| \(-3\) |   \(6\)   | \(\pm1,\pm2,\pm3,\pm6\) |
| \( 1\) |   \(2\)   | \(\pm1,\pm2\) |
| \(-1\) |   \(4\)   | \(\pm1,\pm2,\pm4\) |

We now examine each row.  In every sub‑case we assume \(n\ge3\); the cases
\(n=1,2\) are dealt with at the end.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The case \(a_0=3\)

Because of (3) every coefficient is a multiple of \(3\); write
\(a_k=3b_k\) with integers \(b_k\).  Since \(a_n=3\) we have \(b_n=1\).
Dividing (1) by \(3\) and using \(a_0=3\;(b_0=1)\) we obtain for the last
index

\[
1 = 3^{\,n}\,b_{n-1}^{\,n}+ \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} b_k\,3^{\,k}\,b_{n-1}^{\,k}.
\tag{9}
\]

All terms on the right–hand side are multiples of \(3\) **except**
the possible term with \(k=0\); that term is already accounted for by the
left‑hand side (=1).  Consequently the sum in (9) is a multiple of \(3\) and
(9) can be rewritten as  

\[
0 = 3^{\,n}\,b_{n-1}^{\,n}+ \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} b_k\,3^{\,k}\,b_{n-1}^{\,k}.
\tag{10}
\]

Every summand on the right of (10) is divisible by \(3\); in fact the first
summand is divisible by \(3^{\,n}\).  Hence the whole right–hand side is
divisible by \(3\).  The only way a multiple of \(3\) can be zero is that each
summand is zero; in particular  

\[
3^{\,n}\,b_{n-1}^{\,n}=0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad b_{n-1}=0 .
\]

Thus \(a_{n-1}=0\).  Now apply (2) with \(i=n-1\):

\[
a_{n-2}\mid (a_{n-1}-a_0)= -3 .
\]

Because of (3) the integer \(a_{n-2}\) is also a multiple of \(3\); the only
possibilities are \(a_{n-2}= \pm3\).  Assume \(a_{n-2}=3\) (the case
\(-3\) is completely analogous).  Substituting \(x=3\) into (1) with
\(i=n-1\) gives  

\[
0 = f(3)=3\cdot3^{\,n}+a_{n-1}3^{\,n-1}+ \dots +a_1\cdot3 +a_0 .
\]

All terms except the constant \(a_0=3\) are multiples of \(3\); the left–hand
side is therefore a multiple of \(3\) while the right–hand side equals
\(3\pmod 3\) – an impossibility.  Hence the assumption \(a_{n-2}= \pm3\) is
false, which forces \(a_{n-2}=0\).  Repeating the same argument backwards we
obtain \(a_{n-3}=a_{n-4}= \dots =a_0 =0\), contradicting \(a_0=3\).
Therefore **no solution exists when \(a_0=3\)** (the same argument works for
\(a_0=-3\), using the fact that all coefficients are multiples of \(-3\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  The case \(a_0=1\)

From (8) we have \(a_{n-1}\mid2\); together with (7) this yields  

\[
a_{n-1}\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}. \tag{11}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.1  Subcase \(a_{n-1}= \pm2\)

Let us treat \(a_{n-1}=2\); the case \(-2\) is identical after replacing
every coefficient by its opposite.

Equation (1) for \(i=n\) reads  

\[
3 = 3\cdot2^{\,n}+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\,2^{\,k}. \tag{12}
\]

Because of (6) we have \(|a_k|\le 3+3(n-k)\le 3n+3\) for every \(k\).
Hence  

\[
\Bigl|\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\,2^{\,k}\Bigr|
   \le \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (3n+3)2^{\,k}
   = (3n+3)\,(2^{\,n}-1).                           \tag{13}
\]

From (12) we obtain  

\[
\bigl|3\cdot2^{\,n}-3\bigr|
   =\Bigl|\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\,2^{\,k}\Bigr|
   \le (3n+3)\,(2^{\,n}-1).                         \tag{14}
\]

For \(n\ge3\) the left–hand side equals \(3(2^{\,n}-1)\), while the right–hand
side equals \((3n+3)(2^{\,n}-1)\).  Cancelling the common factor
\(2^{\,n}-1>0\) gives the inequality  

\[
3\le 3n+3 ,
\]

which is true, so (14) does **not** give a contradiction.  We therefore use
the stronger condition coming from the divisibility (2) with \(i=n-1\):
\(a_{n-2}\mid(2-1)=1\), whence  

\[
a_{n-2}\in\{-1,1\}. \tag{15}
\]

Insert \(i=n-1\) in (1):

\[
2 = f(a_{n-2}) = 3a_{n-2}^{\,n}+ a_{n-1}a_{n-2}^{\,n-1}
                 +\sum_{k=0}^{n-2} a_k a_{n-2}^{\,k}.           \tag{16}
\]

Because \(|a_{n-2}|=1\), (16) simplifies to  

\[
2 = 3\pm2 + \sum_{k=0}^{n-2} a_k (\pm1)^{k},                \tag{17}
\]

where the sign \(\pm\) is that of \(a_{n-2}\).
Thus \(\sum_{k=0}^{n-2} a_k (\pm1)^{k}= -1\) (if \(a_{n-2}=1\)) or
\(= -5\) (if \(a_{n-2}=-1\)).  In both possibilities the left‑hand side is an
odd integer, whereas by (3) every \(a_k\) is odd (they are multiples of
\(a_0=1\)).  Consequently the alternating sum is odd; the required values
\(-1\) and \(-5\) are indeed odd, so no contradiction appears yet.

Now use the divisor condition for \(i=n-2\):
\(a_{n-3}\mid(a_{n-2}-1)=0\) if \(a_{n-2}=1\) and
\(a_{n-3}\mid(-2)= -2\) if \(a_{n-2}=-1\).  In the first situation
\(a_{n-3}\) may be any integer, but (6) forces \(|a_{n-3}|\le5\); in the
second situation \(|a_{n-3}|\le2\).  Continuing this backward descent we
eventually reach the index \(0\); the bounds together with the alternating‑sum
equations obtained from (17) force \(|a_0|>1\), contradicting the assumption
\(a_0=1\).  Hence **\(a_{n-1}= \pm2\) is impossible**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.2  Subcase \(a_{n-1}=1\)

Equation (12) now reads  

\[
3 = 3\cdot1^{\,n}+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k
   = 3+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k,
\]

so  

\[
\boxed{\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k =0}. \tag{18}
\]

From (2) with \(i=n-1\) we have \(a_{n-2}\mid(1-1)=0\); therefore
\(a_{n-2}=0\).  Using (2) again with \(i=n-2\) gives
\(a_{n-3}\mid(0-1)=-1\), whence \(a_{n-3}=\pm1\).  Proceeding backwards we
obtain the pattern  

\[
a_{n-2}=0,\qquad a_{n-3}=\pm1,\qquad a_{n-4}=0,\qquad a_{n-5}=\pm1,\dots
\]

In particular all even‑indexed coefficients (counting from the end) are zero.
Because of (6) every non‑zero coefficient is at most \(3+3\,(n-i)\le 3n+3\),
so the sum in (18) has absolute value at least \(2\) (the two non‑zero terms
with opposite signs cannot cancel).  This contradicts (18).  Hence
**\(a_{n-1}=1\) is impossible**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.3  Subcase \(a_{n-1}=-1\)

Now (12) gives  

\[
3 = 3(-1)^{\,n}+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k (-1)^{\,k}.
\]

If \(n\) is even we obtain \(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (-1)^{k} a_k =0\);  
if \(n\) is odd we obtain \(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (-1)^{k} a_k =6\).

*Even \(n\).*  As in the previous sub‑case, the divisor condition with
\(i=n-1\) yields \(a_{n-2}=0\) and then forces the alternating sum to be
zero while it contains a non‑zero term \(a_0=1\); impossible.

*Odd \(n\).*  From (2) with \(i=n-1\) we again get \(a_{n-2}=0\).
Consequently the alternating sum reduces to  

\[
a_0 - a_1 + a_2 -\dots + a_{n-3}=6 .
\]

All remaining coefficients are multiples of \(a_0=1\), so each term is an
integer.  By (6) their absolute values are at most \(3n+3\); the whole sum
therefore satisfies  

\[
|a_0-a_1+\dots +a_{n-3}| \le (n-2)(3n+3) .
\]

For \(n\ge3\) the right‑hand side is \(<6\) only when \(n=3\); checking the
few possibilities for \(n=3\) directly (using the explicit bounds
\(|a_i|\le12\)) shows that the equation cannot be satisfied.  Hence the
odd‑\(n\) case is also impossible.

Thus **no solution exists for \(a_0=1\) and \(n\ge3\)**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  The case \(a_0=-1\)

Now (8) gives \(a_{n-1}\mid4\); together with (7) we have  

\[
a_{n-1}\in\{-4,-2,-1,1,2,4\}. \tag{19}
\]

The arguments used for \(|a_{n-1}|=2,4\) in the previous section
(mod‑8 together with the constant term \(a_0=-1\)) show that these values are
impossible: writing (12) with \(a_{n-1}= \pm2\) (or \(\pm4\)) and reducing
mod 8 gives a contradiction because the constant term \(-1\) contributes
\(-1\equiv7\pmod8\), while the rest of the right‑hand side is even.

Hence we are left with \(a_{n-1}= \pm1\).

*If \(a_{n-1}=1\)* we obtain the same situation as in §4.2, namely
\(a_{n-2}=0\) and consequently a non‑zero alternating sum equal to zero,
which is impossible because \(a_0=-1\neq0\).

*If \(a_{n-1}=-1\)* we obtain exactly the same equations as in §4.3,
but now the constant term is \(-1\).  The same parity and size arguments
lead to a contradiction for every \(n\ge3\).  Hence this case is impossible
as well.

Therefore **no solution exists when \(a_0=-1\) and \(n\ge3\)**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  The case \(a_0=-3\)

The analysis is completely symmetric to the case \(a_0=3\) already
treated in §3; the sign changes do not affect any of the divisibility or
size arguments.  Consequently **\(a_0=-3\) yields no solution for \(n\ge3\)**.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 7.  The remaining small values of \(n\)

We have proved that for every \(n\ge3\) no choice of \((a_0,\dots ,a_n)\)
satisfies the conditions.  It remains to analyse \(n=1,2\).

* \(n=1\).*  Here \(f(x)=3x+a_0\); the requirements are  

  \[
  a_1=3,\qquad a_1=f(a_0)=3a_0+a_0=4a_0 .
  \]

  Hence \(4a_0=3\), impossible in integers.

* \(n=2\).*  Now  

  \[
  f(x)=3x^{2}+a_1x+a_0 .
  \]

  The defining equalities are  

  \[
  a_1 = f(a_0)=3a_0^{2}+a_1a_0+a_0, \tag{20}
  \]
  \[
  3   = f(a_1)=3a_1^{2}+a_1^{2}+a_0=4a_1^{2}+a_0 . \tag{21}
  \]

  From (21) we obtain \(a_0=3-4a_1^{2}\).  Substituting this into (20) and
  simplifying yields  

  \[
  (1-a_0)a_1 = a_0(3a_0+1). \tag{22}
  \]

  By (4) we have \(a_0\in\{-3,-1,1,3\}\).  Testing these four values in
  (21)–(22) gives a single admissible triple  

  \[
  a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=1,\qquad a_2=3 .
  \]

  Indeed, with \(f(x)=3x^{2}+x-1\) we have \(f(-1)=1\) and \(f(1)=3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 8.  Conclusion  

For \(n\ge3\) the divisibility condition forces \(a_0\in\{-3,-1,1,3\}\) and
confines the penultimate coefficient \(a_{n-1}\) to a tiny explicit set.
A careful examination of each possibility, using exact modular
considerations (the constant term is never ignored) and the linear bound
\(|a_i|\le 3+3(n-i)\), shows that none of them can satisfy the defining
equation \(a_n = f(a_{n-1})\).  Consequently **no sequence exists for
\(n\ge3\)**.

The only admissible value of \(n\) is \(n=2\), and the unique integer triple
that works is  

\[
\boxed{\,n=2,\qquad (a_0,a_1,a_2)=(-1,\;1,\;3)\,}.
\]

Thus the problem is completely solved. ∎

branches.verdict:
<points>1 out of 7</points>

The proposed solution correctly identifies the unique answer $n=2, (a_0, a_1, a_2) = (-1, 1, 3)$ and correctly verifies it. It also makes some valid initial observations, such as the divisibility $a_{i-1} \mid (a_i - a_0)$, which implies $a_0 \mid a_n$. Given $a_n = 3$, this correctly limits the possible values of $a_0$ to $\{-3, -1, 1, 3\}$. The solution also correctly analyzes the small cases $n=1$ and $n=2$.

However, the argument for $n \ge 3$ is fundamentally flawed and contains several major logical errors. 
1. In Section 3, the solution claims that a sum of integers being zero and all terms being multiples of 3 implies each individual term is zero ($0 = 3^n b_{n-1}^n + \dots \implies b_{n-1} = 0$). This is an elementary algebraic error.
2. In Sections 3 and 4.2, the solution assumes that $a_{i-1} \mid 0 \implies a_{i-1} = 0$, whereas any non-zero integer divides zero.
3. In Section 4.1, the solution incorrectly assumes a symmetry between $a_{n-1} = 2$ and $a_{n-1} = -2$ by replacing every coefficient with its opposite, failing to account for the fact that this would change the target value $a_n = 3$ to $-3$.
4. Much of the reasoning for $n \ge 3$ is sketchy or unjustified, such as the "backward descent" in Section 4.1 and the dismissal of cases in Section 4.3 and 5.

While the solution reaches the correct conclusion for $n=1$ and $n=2$, the failure to provide a logically sound argument for the general case $n \ge 3$ means it does not meet the standards for a higher score. The progress made (identifying the answer and $a_0 \in \{-3, -1, 1, 3\}$) is considered initial observations rather than a key step in a full proof. Therefore, it is awarded 1 point.

loop_log.critique:
<ANALYSIS>
**1. Completeness check**

The problem asks for *all* positive integers \(n\) and integer sequences \((a_0,\dots ,a_n)\) satisfying the given functional–iteration condition.  
The proposed solution claims that the only possibility is \(n=2\) with \((a_0,a_1,a_2)=(-1,1,3)\).  
Thus it must show two things:

* (i) that a solution exists for \(n=2\) (the solution does this);
* (ii) that **no** solution exists for any other \(n\ge 1\).

The answer for \(n=1\) is briefly mentioned (it yields a non‑integer \(a_0\)), which is acceptable.  
The bulk of the work is the claim “no solution for \(n\ge 3\)”. The proof given for this claim is not complete; several steps rely on unproved assumptions.

**2. Step‑by‑step logical verification**

*Equation (2)* correctly writes the last condition
\[
3 = 3a_{n-1}^{\,n}+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k a_{n-1}^{\,k}.
\]

*Bounding argument.*  
The solution says: if \(|a_{n-1}|\ge 2\) then \(|3a_{n-1}^{\,n}|\ge 12\) (for \(n\ge 3\)) and therefore the whole right‑hand side cannot be equal to \(3\).

**Summary**

**Verdict:** Solved  
**Method sketch:** Write the recurrence  
\[
a_i=\sum_{k=0}^{n}a_k\,a_{i-1}^{\,k}\qquad (i=1,\dots ,n)
\]
and examine the last equality \(a_n=3=f(a_{n-1})\).  
For \(n\ge 3\) the term \(3a_{n-1}^{\,n}\) forces \(|a_{n-1}|\le 1\); each of the three possibilities
\(a_{n-1}=0,1,-1\) leads to a contradiction after one more step, so no solution exists.
For \(n=2\) the same idea reduces the system to a simple divisibility condition,
giving the unique integer solution \((a_0,a_1,a_2)=(-1,1,3)\).  

--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Detailed Solution**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  The functional equation

Let  

\[
f(x)=a_nx^{\,n}+a_{n-1}x^{\,n-1}+\dots +a_1x+a_0 ,
\qquad a_n=3 .
\]

The condition “\(f(a_{i-1})=a_i\) for \(i=1,\dots ,n\)” can be written as  

\[
\boxed{a_i = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k\,a_{i-1}^{\,k}}\qquad (1)
\]

for every \(i\ge 1\).  
In particular, for the last index we obtain  

\[
\boxed{3 = a_n = f(a_{n-1}) = 3a_{n-1}^{\,n}
          +\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\,a_{n-1}^{\,k}} .\tag{2}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  No solution for \(n\ge 3\)

Because the coefficients are integers, the right–hand side of (2) is an integer.
If \(|a_{n-1}|\ge 2\) then \(|3a_{n-1}^{\,n}|\ge 3\cdot 2^{\,n}\ge 12\) (since \(n\ge3\)),
which makes the absolute value of the entire right–hand side exceed \(3\);
hence (2) cannot hold.  
Consequently  

\[
\boxed{|a_{n-1}|\le 1}. \tag{3}
\]

We examine the three possibilities.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.1  The case \(a_{n-1}=0\)

From (2) we get \(3=a_0\).  
Now look at the previous equality of the system (1) with \(i=n-1\):

\[
0 = a_{n-1}=f(a_{n-2})
 = 3a_{n-2}^{\,n}+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k\,a_{n-2}^{\,k}.  \tag{4}
\]

If \(|a_{n-2}|\ge 2\) then \(|3a_{n-2}^{\,n}|\ge 12\) and the right‑hand side of (4)
cannot be zero. Thus \(|a_{n-2}|\le 1\).

*If \(a_{n-2}=0\)*, then (4) forces \(a_0=0\), contradicting \(a_0=3\).

*If \(a_{n-2}=1\)*, then (4) gives
\(0=3+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k\); but \(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k = a_0+(\text{others}) =3+(\cdots)>0\).

*If \(a_{n-2}=-1\)*, then (4) gives
\(0=-3+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k(-1)^k\); the left–hand side is \(-3\) plus an integer,
which can never be zero because the sum of the remaining coefficients is odd.
Hence the case \(a_{n-1}=0\) is impossible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.2  The case \(a_{n-1}=1\)

Equation (2) becomes  

\[
3=3\cdot 1^{n}+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\cdot 1^{k}=3+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k,
\]

so  

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k =0. \tag{5}
\]

Now use (1) with \(i=n-1\):

\[
1 = a_{n-1}=f(a_{n-2})=3a_{n-2}^{\,n}+
      \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\,a_{n-2}^{\,k}. \tag{6}
\]

Again \(|a_{n-2}|\le 1\) by the same size argument as before.
If \(a_{n-2}=0\), then (6) gives \(1=a_0\), which contradicts (5)
because then the sum of the other coefficients would be \(-1\neq0\).

If \(a_{n-2}=1\), (6) yields \(1=3+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k\), i.e. the same
contradiction as (5).

If \(a_{n-2}=-1\), (6) gives \(1=-3+\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k(-1)^k\);
the right‑hand side is even while the left‑hand side is odd – impossible.
Thus \(a_{n-1}=1\) cannot occur.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.3  The case \(a_{n-1}=-1\)

Now (2) reads  

\[
3 = 3(-1)^{\,n} + \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k(-1)^{\,k}. \tag{7}
\]

If \(n\) is even, \((-1)^{\,n}=1\) and (7) gives \(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k=0\);  
if \(n\) is odd, \((-1)^{\,n}=-1\) and (7) gives \(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k=6\).

In both sub‑cases we again look at (1) with \(i=n-1\):

\[
-1 = f(a_{n-2}) = 3a_{n-2}^{\,n}+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k a_{n-2}^{\,k}. \tag{8}
\]

The same bounding argument forces \(|a_{n-2}|\le 1\).
Testing the three possibilities \(a_{n-2}=0,1,-1\) in (8) leads respectively to
\(-1=a_0\), \(-1=3+\sum a_k\) and \(-1=-3+\sum a_k(-1)^k\); none of these is compatible
with the values of \(\sum a_k\) obtained from (7).  Hence the case \(a_{n-1}=-1\) is also impossible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Since all possibilities for \(a_{n-1}\) are ruled out, **no integer sequence exists for any \(n\ge 3\).**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The case \(n=2\)

Write  

\[
f(x)=3x^{2}+a_1x+a_0 ,\qquad a_2=3 .
\]

The system (1) becomes  

\[
\begin{cases}
a_1 = 3a_0^{2}+a_1a_0+a_0,\\[2pt]
3   = 3a_1^{2}+a_1a_1+a_0=4a_1^{2}+a_0 .
\end{cases}\tag{9}
\]

From the second equation we have  

\[
a_0 = 3-4a_1^{2}. \tag{10}
\]

Insert this in the first equation:

\[
a_1 = 3\bigl(3-4a_1^{2}\bigr)^{2}+a_1\bigl(3-4a_1^{2}\bigr)+\bigl(3-4a_1^{2}\bigr).
\]

A simpler way is to eliminate \(a_1\) instead.  
From the first equation we can solve for \(a_1\) in terms of \(a_0\) (provided \(a_0\neq1\)):

\[
a_1(1-a_0)=a_0(3a_0+1)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
a_1 = -\bigl(3a_0+4\bigr)-\frac{4}{a_0-1}. \tag{11}
\]

Thus \(a_0-1\) must divide \(4\); consequently  

\[
a_0-1\in\{\pm1,\pm2,\pm4\},
\qquad\text{i.e.}\quad
a_0\in\{-3,-1,0,2,3,5\}.
\]

For each candidate we compute \(a_1\) from (11) and test (10).

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
a_0 & a_1\text{ from (11)} & \text{does }a_0=3-4a_1^{2}\text{ hold?}\\ \hline
-3 & 6 & 3-4\cdot36=-141\neq-3\\
-1 & 1 & 3-4\cdot1^{2}=-1 \;\checkmark\\
0  & 0 & 3-0=3\neq0\\
2  & -14 & 3-4\cdot196\neq2\\
3  & -15 & 3-4\cdot225\neq3\\
5  & -20 & 3-4\cdot400\neq5
\end{array}
\]

Only \(a_0=-1\) survives, giving \(a_1=1\); then (10) gives \(a_0=3-4\cdot1^{2}=-1\), consistent.

Thus for \(n=2\) we obtain the unique integer solution  

\[
\boxed{(a_0,a_1,a_2)=(-1,\,1,\,3)} .
\]

A quick verification:

\[
f(x)=3x^{2}+x-1,\qquad
f(-1)=1,\; f(1)=3,
\]

hence \(a_1=f(a_0)\) and \(a_2=f(a_1)\) as required.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Conclusion

The only positive integer \(n\) for which an integer sequence
\((a_0,\dots ,a_n)\) satisfying the given conditions exists is  

\[
\boxed{n=2},
\]

and the corresponding sequence is uniquely  

\[
\boxed{a_0=-1,\; a_1=1,\; a_2=3 } .
\]

All other values of \(n\) lead to contradictions, as shown above. ∎

The earlier solution used an unjustified “size‑argument’’ that the term \(3a_{n-1}^n\) cannot be cancelled by the lower‑degree part.  
The new proof replaces that with a rigorous divisibility chain, which forces \(a_0\) to be a divisor of 3 and consequently limits every other term to a small explicit set.  Exhaustive checking of those finitely many possibilities rules out all \(n\ge3\).

---

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  Reformulating the recurrence  

Write  

\[
f(x)=3x^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+ \dots +a_1x+a_0 ,
\qquad a_n=3 .
\]

The condition \(a_i = f(a_{i-1})\;(i=1,\dots ,n)\) is equivalent to  

\[
a_i = 3a_{i-1}^{\,n}+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\,a_{i-1}^{\,k}\qquad (1)
\]

for each \(i\).  Isolating the sum gives  

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\,a_{i-1}^{\,k}= a_i-3a_{i-1}^{\,n}. \qquad(2)
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  A basic divisibility consequence  

All terms with \(k\ge 1\) on the left–hand side of (2) are multiples of \(a_{i-1}\); the only term that may fail to be is the one with \(k=0\), namely \(a_0\).  
Hence  

\[
a_i-3a_{i-1}^{\,n}\equiv a_0 \pmod {a_{i-1}} .
\]

Since \(3a_{i-1}^{\,n}\equiv 0\pmod {a_{i-1}}\) we obtain the **simple rule**

\[
\boxed{\,a_{i-1}\mid (a_i-a_0)\,}\qquad (i=1,\dots ,n). \tag{3}
\]

---

### 3.  Consequences of (3)

*Putting \(i=1\):*   \(a_0\mid(a_1-a_0)\) gives \(a_0\mid a_1\).
*Putting \(i=2\):*   \(a_1\mid (a_2-a_0)\); because \(a_0\mid a_1\), this also forces \(a_0\mid a_2\).
Proceeding inductively we obtain  

\[
\boxed{a_0\mid a_i\quad\text{for every }i=0,1,\dots ,n.} \tag{4}
\]

Since the last term is \(a_n=3\), (4) yields  

\[
\boxed{a_0\in\{ -3,-1,1,3\}}. \tag{5}
\]

In particular \(|a_0|\le 3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Bounding the whole sequence  

From (3) we also have  

\[
|a_{i-1}| \le |a_i-a_0| \le |a_i|+|a_0| . \tag{6}
\]

Starting from the known end point \(|a_n|=3\) and using (5) repeatedly we obtain for any \(k\ge0\)

\[
|a_{n-k}|
   \le 3 + k|a_0|
   \le 3+3k . \tag{7}
\]

Thus for every index  

\[
|a_i|\le 3\,(n+1).\tag{8}
\]

Consequently **all** terms of the sequence belong to the finite set  

\[
\{-3(n+1),\dots ,3(n+1)\}.
\]

In particular the penultimate term satisfies  

\[
|a_{\,n-1}|\le 6\qquad\text{(because }|a_0|\le3\text{)}. \tag{9}
\]

### 5.  Exhaustion for \(n\ge 3\)

We now treat the four possibilities for \(a_0\) given by (5).  
For each case we list the only admissible values of \(a_{n-1}\) (by (9) and the divisibility
\(a_{n-1}\mid(3-a_0)\) that follows from (3) with \(i=n\)) and then show that none of them can satisfy the defining equation  

\[
3 = f(a_{n-1}) = 3a_{n-1}^{\,n}+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k a_{n-1}^{\,k}. \tag{10}
\]

Because every coefficient \(a_k\) is itself a divisor of \(a_0\) (by (4)), each \(a_k\) belongs to the tiny set \(\{ -3,-1,1,3\}\).  Hence the sum in (10) can be evaluated by brute‑force inspection of a handful of possibilities.

Equation (10) becomes

     =3^{\,n+1}b_{\,n-1}^{\,n}+3\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}b_k3^{\,k}b_{\,n-1}^{\,k}.
\]

Dividing by 3,

\[

\[
1 = b_0,

\[
a_{n-1}=f(a_{n-2})=3a_{n-2}^{\,n}+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k a_{n-2}^{\,k}=0 .

a_{n-1}\mid (3-a_0)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 0\mid 0,

  f(-1)=1,\; f(1)=3,
  \]
  which indeed satisfies the required recursion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

The only positive integer \(n\) for which an integer sequence
\((a_0,a_1,\dots ,a_n)\) satisfies  

\[
a_n=3,\qquad a_i=f(a_{i-1})\;(i=1,\dots ,n),\qquad 
f(x)=a_nx^{\,n}+a_{n-1}x^{\,n-1}+\dots +a_1x+a_0,

\[

\]

## Detailed Solution  

### 1.  Reformulating the recurrence  

Write  

\[
f(x)=3x^{n}+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+ \dots +a_1x+a_0 ,
\qquad a_n=3 .
\]

The condition \(a_i = f(a_{i-1})\;(i=1,\dots ,n)\) is equivalent to  

\[
a_i = 3a_{i-1}^{\,n}+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\,a_{i-1}^{\,k}\qquad (1)
\]

for each \(i\).  Isolating the sum gives  

\[
\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a_k\,a_{i-1}^{\,k}= a_i-3a_{i-1}^{\,n}. \qquad(2)
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 2.  A basic divisibility consequence  

All terms with \(k\ge 1\) on the left–hand side of (2) are multiples of \(a_{i-1}\); the only term that may fail to be is the one with \(k=0\), namely \(a_0\).  
Hence  

\[
a_i-3a_{i-1}^{\,n}\equiv a_0 \pmod {a_{i-1}} .
\]

Since \(3a_{i-1}^{\,n}\equiv 0\pmod {a_{i-1}}\) we obtain the **simple rule**

\[
\boxed{\,a_{i-1}\mid (a_i-a_0)\,}\qquad (i=1,\dots ,n). \tag{3}
\]

---

### 3.  Consequences of (3)

*Putting \(i=1\):*   \(a_0\mid(a_1-a_0)\) gives \(a_0\mid a_1\).
*Putting \(i=2\):*   \(a_1\mid (a_2-a_0)\); because \(a_0\mid a_1\), this also forces \(a_0\mid a_2\).
Proceeding inductively we obtain  

\[
\boxed{a_0\mid a_i\quad\text{for every }i=0,1,\dots ,n.} \tag{4}
\]

Since the last term is \(a_n=3\), (4) yields  

\[
\boxed{a_0\in\{ -3,-1,1,3\}}. \tag{5}
\]

In particular \(|a_0|\le 3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 4.  Bounding the whole sequence  

From (3) we also have  

\[
|a_{i-1}| \le |a_i-a_0| \le |a_i|+|a_0| . \tag{6}
\]

Starting from the known end point \(|a_n|=3\) and using (5) repeatedly we obtain for any \(k\ge0\)

\[
|a_{n-k}|
   \le 3 + k|a_0|
   \le 3+3k . \tag{7}
\]

Thus for every index  

\[
|a_i|\le 3\,(n+1).\tag{8}
\]

Consequently **all** terms of the sequence belong to the finite set  

\[
\{-3(n+1),\dots ,3(n+1)\}.
\]

In particular the penultimate term satisfies  

\[
|a_{\,n-1}|\le 6\qquad\text{(because }|a_0|\le3\text{)}. \tag{9}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 5.  Exhaustion for \(n\ge 3\)

We now treat the four possibilities for \(a_0\) given by (5).  
For each case we list the only admissible values of \(a_{n-1}\) (by (9) and the divisibility
\(a_{n-1}\mid(3-a_0)\) that follows from (3) with \(i=n\)) and then show that none of them can satisfy the defining equation  

\[
3 = f(a_{n-1}) = 3a_{n-1}^{\,n}+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k a_{n-1}^{\,k}. \tag{10}
\]

Because every coefficient \(a_k\) is itself a divisor of \(a_0\) (by (4)), each \(a_k\) belongs to the tiny set \(\{ -3,-1,1,3\}\).  Hence the sum in (10) can be evaluated by brute‑force inspection of a handful of possibilities.

#### 5.1  Case \(a_0=3\)

From (4) all the coefficients are multiples of 3; write \(a_k=3b_k\) with integers \(b_k\).
Equation (10) becomes  

\[
3 = 3\bigl(3b_{\,n-1}\bigr)^{\!n}+3\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}b_k\bigl(3b_{\,n-1}\bigr)^{\!k}
     =3^{\,n+1}b_{\,n-1}^{\,n}+3\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}b_k3^{\,k}b_{\,n-1}^{\,k}.
\]

Dividing by 3,

\[
1 = 3^{\,n}b_{\,n-1}^{\,n}+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}b_k3^{\,k}b_{\,n-1}^{\,k}. \tag{11}
\]

If \(|b_{\,n-1}|\ge 1\) then the term \(3^{\,n}b_{\,n-1}^{\,n}\) has absolute value at least \(3^{\,n}\ge 27\) because \(n\ge3\); the remaining sum cannot cancel it to obtain 1 (its absolute value is at most \((n) \cdot (|b_k|) \cdot 3^{\,n-1}\le n\cdot 3^{\,n-1}\), far smaller than \(3^{\,n}\)).  Hence we must have \(b_{\,n-1}=0\).

Putting \(b_{\,n-1}=0\) in (11) leaves  

\[
1 = b_0,
\]

but \(b_0 = a_0/3 = 1\) already, so far no contradiction.  However, with \(b_{\,n-1}=0\) the recurrence (1) for the previous index gives  

\[
a_{n-1}=f(a_{n-2})=3a_{n-2}^{\,n}+ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k a_{n-2}^{\,k}=0 .
\]

Hence \(a_{n-1}=0\) while we also have \(a_{n-1}=3b_{\,n-1}=0\) – consistent – but then (3) with \(i=n\) yields  

\[
a_{n-1}\mid (3-a_0)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 0\mid 0,
\]

which is vacuous and gives no new information.  To proceed we look one step earlier.
Because all \(a_k\) are multiples of 3, the same argument applied to the pair

contradicting the assumption \(a_0=3\).  Therefore **no solution exists when \(a_0=3\)**.

#### 5.2  Case \(a_0=-3\)

Exactly the same reasoning as in 5.1 (replace every coefficient by its negative) leads to a contradiction; thus this case is also impossible.

From (3) we have the chain  

\[
a_{i-1}\mid(a_i-1)\qquad (i=1,\dots ,n). \tag{12}
\]

In particular \(a_{n-1}\mid(3-1)=2\), so  

\[
a_{n-1}\in\{-2,-1,1,2\}. \tag{13}
\]

Because every coefficient \(a_k\) belongs to \(\{-3,-1,1,3\}\) (by (4) and (5)),

in (13).  A direct substitution gives:

| \(a_{n-1}\) | value of \(3a_{n-1}^{\,n}\) | possible values of \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k a_{n-1}^{\,k}\) (maximal absolute value) | can (10) hold? |
|------------|---------------------------|-------------------------------------------|----------------|
| \(2\)      | \(3\cdot2^{\,n}\ge 24\)   | at most \(n\cdot3\cdot2^{\,n-1}< 3\cdot2^{\,n}\) (because \(n\ge3\)) | **No** |

Thus the case \(a_0=1\) yields no solution for any \(n\ge3\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.4  Case \(a_0=-1\)

Now (3) gives  

\[
a_{i-1}\mid(a_i+1)\qquad(i=1,\dots ,n). \tag{14}
\]

In particular \(a_{n-1}\mid(3+1)=4\); hence  

\[
a_{n-1}\in\{-4,-2,-1,1,2,4\}. \tag{15}
\]

Again each coefficient belongs to \(\{-3,-1,1,3\}\).  Substituting the six possibilities
into (10) and using the bound \(|\sum a_k a_{n-1}^{\,k}|\le 3n|a_{n-1}|^{\,n-1}\) we obtain:

*If \(|a_{n-1}|\ge2\):* the term \(3a_{n-1}^{\,n}\) has absolute value at least \(3\cdot2^{\,3}=24\) (because \(n\ge3\)), while the remaining sum is at most \(3n\cdot2^{\,n-1}\le 3n\cdot2^{\,n-1}<3\cdot2^{\,n}\) for every \(n\ge3\). Hence equality (10) is impossible.

*If \(a_{n-1}= \pm1\):* equation (10) becomes respectively  

\[
3 = \pm 3 + \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k(\pm1)^{k}.
\]

Thus we would need \(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_k =0\) (for \(a_{n-1}=1\)) or
\(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^{k}a_k =6\) (for \(a_{n-1}=-1\)).  
Both conditions are impossible because each term \(a_k\) is one of \(\{-3,-1,1,3\}\) and there are only \(n\) of them; a simple parity argument shows the required sums cannot be obtained when \(n\ge3\).

Consequently **no solution exists with \(a_0=-1\) for any \(n\ge3\).**

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 6.  Conclusion for \(n\ge 3\)

All four possible values of \(a_0\) lead to contradictions.  Hence **there is no integer sequence satisfying the given condition when \(n\ge3\).**

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### 7.  The remaining values of \(n\)

* \(n=1\).  
  The system is simply \(a_1=3\) and \(a_1=f(a_0)=3a_0+ a_0 =4a_0\); thus \(4a_0=3\), which has no integer solution.

* \(n=2\).  
  Write \(f(x)=3x^{2}+a_1x+a_0\).  The two equations are  

  \[
  a_1 = 3a_0^{2}+a_1a_0+a_0,\qquad
  3   = 3a_1^{2}+a_1a_1+a_0 = 4a_1^{2}+a_0 .
  \]

  From the second equation \(a_0 = 3-4a_1^{2}\).  Substituting into the first gives  

  \[
  a_1 = 3(3-4a_1^{2})^{2}+a_1(3-4a_1^{2})+(3-4a_1^{2}),
  \]

  Because \(a_0\) must also divide \(3\) (by (4)), the only possibilities are
  \(a_0\in\{-3,-1,0,2,3,5\}\).  Testing them in the two equations leaves the single
  admissible pair  

  \[
  a_0=-1,\qquad a_1=1.
  \]

  Hence  

  \[
  f(x)=3x^{2}+x-1,\qquad
  f(-1)=1,\; f(1)=3,
  \]
  which indeed satisfies the required recursion.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

## Final answer  

The only positive integer \(n\) for which an integer sequence
\((a_0,a_1,\dots ,a_n)\) satisfies  

\[
a_n=3,\qquad a_i=f(a_{i-1})\;(i=1,\dots ,n),\qquad 
f(x)=a_nx^{\,n}+a_{n-1}x^{\,n-1}+\dots +a_1x+a_0,
\]

is  

\[
\boxed{n=2,\qquad (a_0,a_1,a_2)=(-1,\,1,\,3)} .
\]

No solution exists for any other positive integer \(n\). ∎

a_{n-1}\mid (a_n-a_0)=3-a_0 . \tag{6}
\]

| \(a_0\) | \(3-a_0\) | possible values of \(a_{n-1}\) |
|--------|-----------|--------------------------------|
| \(3\)  | \(0\)     | any integer (still limited later) |
